mcqs.question: In TF-IDF, why does a term like "the" contribute almost no score even if it appears in a document many times?
options: TF-IDF ignores term frequency entirely
Common words are removed from the index before scoring even begins
Its inverse document frequency (IDF) is very low because it appears in nearly every document, dragging the combined score down
TF-IDF only scores the first occurrence of any term
mcqs.explanation: IDF measures rarity across the collection; a word appearing in almost every document has very low IDF, so multiplying it by term frequency still yields a low score. TF-IDF does use frequency, and stop-word removal is a separate preprocessing step, not why IDF works.

mcqs.question: What two problems does BM25 fix relative to plain TF-IDF?
options: It removes the need for an inverted index entirely
It adds support for multi-language queries and nothing else
It replaces term frequency with document popularity
It saturates the effect of raw term frequency and normalizes for document length
mcqs.explanation: BM25 caps the diminishing returns of repeated term mentions and adjusts scores relative to a document's length against the collection average — both practical gaps in plain TF-IDF. It still relies on an inverted index and isn't primarily about language or popularity.

mcqs.question: A new search product just launched with no usage data yet. Which ranking approach should it start with?
options: Sort strictly by document creation date
Learning-to-rank trained on historical click data
BM25 with a few hand-tuned boosting signals
No ranking at all — return matches in arbitrary order
mcqs.explanation: Learning-to-rank needs enough click/behavior data to train on, which a brand-new product doesn't have. BM25 plus manual boosts needs no training data and works from day one; unordered or date-only results ignore relevance entirely.

mcqs.question: A news search sorts results purely by publish date, and users complain the top result is often barely related to their query. What's the fix?
options: Remove all articles older than a week from the index
Blend recency as one weighted signal alongside text relevance (like BM25), instead of using it as the sole sort key
Switch to sorting by article length instead
Disable ranking and show results in random order
mcqs.explanation: Recency is a useful signal but not a substitute for relevance — combining it with a text-relevance score keeps results both fresh and on-topic. Removing old articles or sorting by length don't address the underlying relevance gap.

mcqs.question: A short 80-word document mentions a rare query term twice; a 1,200-word document mentions the same term 8 times. Why doesn't the longer document automatically score 4x higher?
options: BM25's length normalization discounts raw term frequency relative to how long the document is, since longer text is expected to mention words more often anyway
Longer documents are always excluded from ranking entirely
BM25 ignores document length completely and only compares raw counts
The rare term's IDF value changes based on which document contains it
mcqs.explanation: Length normalization is exactly what prevents raw mention counts from dominating the score — a document 15x longer is expected to have more incidental mentions, so its counts get discounted relative to the collection's average length. IDF is a collection-wide property of the term, not something that varies per document, and BM25 explicitly accounts for length rather than ignoring it.
